articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: Saudi authorities say the latest attack on the international airport in the capital, Riyadh, has killed 12 people and injured over 300. Their statement says the dead on Saturday included four Saudi citizens as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said some of those injured were in critical condition. The attack — the latest of several in the past week on King Khalid International Airport — is expected to increase Saudi pressure on allies including the United States to provide military support for the kingdom.
articles.title: Attack on Riyadh airport killed 12 people and wounded over 300 more, Saudi authorities say

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.
articles.title: Trump weighs joining the fight against Houthis after Riyadh airport attack

articles.author: Anastasia Tsioulcas
articles.description: The center's executive director has named an agent who has worked with ZZ Top and Motley Crue drummer Tommy Lee as the head of programming for the arts institution.
articles.title: The Kennedy Center names new artistic director, amid concerns

articles.author: Bill Chappell
articles.description: Hurricane Isaias is blamed for at least two deaths, after the storm made landfall on the Florida coast and ran through Alabama. There are numerous reports of downed trees, with hundreds of thousands of people without power.
articles.title: At least 2 deaths attributed to Isaias after hurricane bashes Florida and Alabama

articles.author: Yuki Noguchi
articles.description: Scant data about serious adverse effects makes it harder to answer scientific and legal questions about how often the drugs might cause serious harm like blindness or pancreatitis.
articles.title: Ongoing lawsuits allege GLP-1s can cause serious harm. But we don't know how often

articles.author: Claudia Grisales
articles.description: Democrats are hoping to win back Latino voters who have soured on both parties. They hope Latino content creators will bridge the gap.
articles.title: After losing ground with Latino voters, Democrats are turning to influencers for help

articles.author: Malaka Gharib
articles.description: Carve a pumpkin? You can do better than that. Fun and unusual ways to celebrate the season, from writing a gratitude letter to making an ancestral altar.
articles.title: 16 cozy activities to add to your fall bucket list

articles.author: Anastasia Tsioulcas
articles.description: In a blockbuster show, The Metropolitan Museum of Art places the work of two major 20th century artists side by side: the married couple Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock.
articles.title: The Met puts a modern artist front and center (and there's some Jackson Pollock, too)

articles.author: Anas Baba
articles.description: It has been one year since Hamas released the remaining Israeli hostages and President Trump promised an end to the war, but Palestinians say the past 12 months have been a ceasefire in name only.
articles.title: Photos: What a year of ceasefire in Gaza looks like

articles.author: The Associated Press
articles.description: The protests focus on the Election Commission's voter list revision, which the opposition claims disenfranchises millions. The government denies the allegations, saying the revision aims to eliminate duplicate entries.
articles.title: India cracks down on youth protests as anger grows against Modi and election chief

articles.author: Ben Smee
articles.description:
Club issues brief statement about Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, saying latter suffered minor cut to head after a fall
Carlton football club has said two of its players, Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward, required treatment in hospital on Sunday morning in “separate circumstances”.
The club released a statement on Sunday after reports in several media outlets that unnamed players had been taken to hospital by ambulance after a night out. Guardian Australia contacted Carlton seeking comment on the reports.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Two Carlton players treated in hospital after needing care for ‘separate circumstances’

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Rachel Jupp takes role as corporation grapples with digital transformation, a cash crisis and its public service role
With looming job cuts and an ongoing pay dispute, there has not been much to smile about for BBC journalists working in “the pit” – their pet name for the newsroom deep in the belly of New Broadcasting House.
On Monday afternoon, however, they were greeted by a grinning figure conducting a tour of the news floor. She was Rachel Jupp, the BBC’s newly appointed director of news and current affairs. Jupp engaged in a series of polite if brief conversations with her new troops.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Restore the authority’: the challenge for the BBC’s new director of news

articles.author: Matthew Taylor
articles.description:
NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers
Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.
Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had a devastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Research challenges the notion that the growing visibility of crosses and other symbols reflects a revival of Christianity 
Christian nationalism in Britain is being driven largely by people who rarely attend church and are more concerned with defending the country’s Christian heritage, according to research.
The report, by the thinktank Theos, identified five different groups within the UK in a survey that looked at their attitudes to Christianity and Britishness.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

articles.author: Ed Pilkington
articles.description:
Trump has used the full might of the presidency to supercharge executions, but an avalanche of mishaps has put the system’s flaws in the spotlight
It took more than an hour to establish the two intravenous lines through which Christa Pike would be injected with a giant and normally lethal dose of the sedative pentobarbital, and in that time she did everything she could to assist those who were attempting to kill her.
“Please try here,” she said over and over again to Tennessee’s execution team, pointing to specific parts of her body where she thought they might find a vein as they repeatedly stabbed her with needles. “Please try here, I think it will be OK. Please try up on my shoulder, higher.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Capital punishment is surging in the US – but after Christa Pike’s botched execution, what is its future?

articles.author: Australian Associated Press
articles.description:
Kenyan breaks Melbourne Marathon record by two seconds

‘I’m happy to run with the gen Zs,’ 41-year-old says

Marathon’s greatest competitor, Eliud Kipchoge, has sent a message to the next generation declaring that he’s not done yet.
The 41-year-old Kenyan revelled in his Melbourne Marathon debut on Sunday, breaking the race record and delighting thousands of fans at the MCG finish.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘My body is still peaking’: Eliud Kipchoge wins first marathon in three years

articles.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Deceased were all members of the same family, officials say, and one of victims placed the initial emergency call
Five people were shot and killed in an apparent murder-suicide at a residence in Georgia on Friday, authorities say.
The deceased were family members who lived at the home in Douglas, a city in south Georgia.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Five people shot and killed in apparent murder-suicide, Georgia police say

articles.author: Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor and agencies
articles.description:
Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
The latest attack on the international airport in Saudi Arabia’s capital of Riyadh killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others, civil aviation authorities said early Sunday, with some in a critical condition. A Saudi-led coalition blamed Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouring Yemen.
A missile struck a King Khalid international airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport

articles.author: Marina Dunbar and Uwa Ede-Osifo
articles.description:
Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat
A man fatally shot eight people, including a pregnant woman and children, at a Pennsylvania residence on Friday before killing himself, police say.
The victims have not been publicly identified, but seven relatives and a family friend died in the rampage.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania

articles.author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez and agencies
articles.description:
Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
At least four people were reported dead on Saturday amid Isaias after it made landfall late on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities.
The storm also took down trees, knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands and flooded highways – but as Saturday evening approached, the region was reopening.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.
Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights

articles.author: Marina Dunbar (now); José Olivares and Taz Ali (earlier)
articles.description:
This liveblog is now closed. Read the full story here

Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias

Sign up for the US Breaking News email

Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said no requests for search and rescue assistance had been received following Isaias, which he described as “cautiously, a good sign”.
Speaking to Fox News, he said:
I think that may be a sign that people heeded the warnings, took proper precautions. We sure would love to say we have not gotten a report of a fatality yet, and we’ll see what happens.
There’s also a lot of hazards post-storm that people should be careful of, but so far we’ve had a lot of assets in place that have not been called on, which is a good sign. I’d rather be over-prepared, and not have to use them, than not have what you need.”
Hurricane Isaias has weakened to a post-tropical cyclone early Saturday, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said, after it made landfall in Florida and lashed the US Gulf coast with heavy rain and fierce winds.
The category 2 hurricane hit the coast near Destin, Florida, late on Friday, with maximum sustained winds of 105mph.
The storm is expected to move across Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley, the NHC added, with maximum sustained winds decreased to near 35mph.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Hurricane Isaias updates: at least four people dead and hundreds of thousands without power – as it happened

articles.author: Oliver Holmes
articles.description:
US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Donald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel.
The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia

articles.author: Josh Butler
articles.description:
Cooperation between One Nation and the Liberals ‘up to Angus Taylor’, Hanson says at conservative conference. How would that work?

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

The annual Conservative Political Action Conference billed itself as a chance for the leaders of the three main conservative parties – Liberals, Nationals and One Nation – to make their pitch and compete for rightwing voters.
The reception they received in Brisbane on Saturday suggests Pauline Hanson is effectively the preferred opposition leader, with Angus Taylor relegated to leading a minor party.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pauline Hanson seems more and more like the de facto opposition leader. At CPAC, Angus Taylor warmed the seat for her

articles.author: Krishani Dhanji
articles.description:
Expert says declining numbers are causing ‘massive problems’ as international students are ‘basically the only profitable aspect of university operations’

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

University leaders warn they’re struggling to fill international student places due to visa uncertainty and heated political debate on immigration, with regional areas hit the hardest amid concern that financial deficits could affect domestic students.
The latest numbers from the Department of Education in October show on average universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated places, and just five public universities have reached more than 80% capacity, all in capital cities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Regional universities struggle to enrol international students amid visa refusals and heated political rhetoric

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said.
Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, and was set upon by the tiger.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
articles.description:
Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.
The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’

articles.author: Agence France-Presse
articles.description:
Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes
A businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.
The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi
articles.description:
Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
Indian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.
Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown

articles.author: Lorenzo Tondo in Palermo
articles.description:
Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean
Two tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.
A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily

articles.author: Robert Tait in Washington, and Oliver Holmes
articles.description:
US president says agreement needed to lower fuel prices, but move likely to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Donald Trump is on a fresh collision course with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.
Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Vladimir Putin on Friday, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel

articles.author: Angelique Chrisafis in Sevran
articles.description:
Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
On a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-income banlieue town in the suburbs north-east of Paris.
“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state

articles.author: Shaun Walker
articles.description:
Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?
Shortly after 1am one night in April 2019, a CIA officer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.
The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die

articles.author: Robert Mackey
articles.description:
President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’
Donald Trump complained on Friday about not winning the Nobel peace prize for 2026, a year in which he started a war with Iran.
At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech to airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes Norway

articles.author: Graham Readfearn and Agence France-Press
articles.description:
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, 30 and 33, and friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were killed on a surfing trip in 2024

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The parents of Australian surfing brothers murdered in Mexico have said “no outcome can ever undo this tragedy” after three men were convicted of the 2024 killings.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three men found guilty of murders of Australian surfer brothers and US friend in Mexico

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
The quake caused buildings and roads to collapse but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths
A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The US Geological Survey (USGS) said the ⁠earthquake hit at a depth of ⁠12.6km (7.8 miles), with an ​epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200km (124 miles) from the capital, Panama City. It lasted about a minute.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake strikes Panama and triggers panic in capital

articles.author: Tess Ikonomou
articles.description:
With GLP-1s to treat the condition not specifically approved by the TGA, patients are being prescribed them off-label

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Women living with a chronic hormonal condition should have access to taxpayer-funded weight-loss medications, advocates say.
The Polyendrocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome Association of Australia (POSAA) is urging for GLP-1 drugs to be approved on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme for people living with the condition.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Women with PMOS should get subsidised weight-loss drugs, Australian advocates say

articles.author: Melody Schreiber
articles.description:
Recommended dose of hepatitis B vaccine will be withheld from thousands of newborns by Danish researchers
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.
It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Controversial vaccine trial touted by RFK Jr gets go-ahead in Guinea-Bissau

articles.author: Jason Burke, international security correspondent
articles.description:
Hammam al-Hammami is believed to have been targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion airport near Tel Aviv
The co-pilot who tried to seize control of a passenger jet flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week was planning to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Israel’s international airport, prosecutors in the United Arab Emirates said on Friday.
Hammam al-Hammami attacked the plane’s Indian pilot with an emergency axe, but failed to prevent his badly injured colleague from opening the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower his assailant.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Flydubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Israeli airport, UAE prosecutors say

articles.author: Julian Borger and Rachel Savage
articles.description:
Committee recognises work of South African who chaired UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza

The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.
The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law

articles.author: Jason Burke
articles.description:
Only Iran and Afghanistan routinely carry out sentences in public, with Saudi Arabia appearing to have ended practice

US politics – live updates

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.
Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company

articles.author: Adam Morton in Nadi, Fiji
articles.description:
‘The climate issue is the security issue,’ says Turkish minister at Pacific pre-Cop summit in Fiji
Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.
But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence

articles.author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
articles.description:
Storm expected to make landfall on US’s northern Gulf coast with risk of flash floods and isolated river flooding
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Attack is deadliest in kingdom since it launched major military offensive with allies against Houthis in Yemen
Three Saudi citizens have been killed and several other people were wounded in attacks targeting Riyadh ⁠airport for which Yemen’s Houthis claimed responsibility, Saudi officials have said.
The attack late on Thursday was the deadliest in Saudi Arabia since the kingdom and allied forces in neighbouring Yemen launched a major military offensive last weekend against the Iran-backed Houthis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Three Saudis killed in Riyadh airport attack claimed by Houthis

articles.author: Nino Bucci Courts and justice reporter
articles.description:
Employee had also been in Bali when he told his manager he was working from home, Fair Work Commission hears

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.
The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case

articles.author: Saher Ahmed in Cairo
articles.description:
Matsadaash staff allege torture and forced confessions after being held on charges of working for Muslim Brotherhood
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.
Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues

articles.author: Pippa Neill Environment reporter
articles.description:
Species with leaves large enough to be seen from space is already critically endangered – and plans are afoot to protect it
A chance social media encounter has led to the race-against-time discovery of a new species of giant waterlily that has until now been hidden in the depths of Colombia’s jungle.
But the plant, which is so huge it is visible from space, is already considered critically endangered.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How a plant selfie in Colombian jungle led to ‘jaw dropping’ giant waterlily find

articles.author: Guardian staff and agencies
articles.description:
Thousands expected to march in Delhi on Saturday, as anger mounts over controversial changes to voter lists in world’s largest democracy 
India’s Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which began as a satirical movement but is now emerging as a political force among gen Z’s, says authorities have begun detaining its members en masse days before a major anti-government protest in Delhi.
Opposition parties, their student units, and the “Cockroach” youth movement have been holding almost daily demonstrations seeking the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over a controversial revision of ⁠voter lists.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s ‘Cockroach’ party accuses government of mass detention of members ahead of weekend protest

articles.author: South West News Service
articles.description:
Free-roaming Aldabra population far exceeds human population of Seychelles after decades-long recovery programme
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.
A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island

articles.author: Raphael Rashid in Seoul
articles.description:
Responding to a Guardian report that revealed thousands of tonnes of fuel was transported to Russia, Seoul said it was investigating the cases
South Korea will take legal action if it finds that shipments of fuel from its ports to Russia broke domestic law, the government has said, responding to a Guardian report on the trade.
The government, in a statement issued by the foreign and trade ministries and the customs service, said that it is “checking additional information concerning the loading cases reported by the Guardian” and “if the verification establishes that our laws and regulations have been violated, it plans to act in accordance with the law”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: South Korea threatens legal action if fuel shipments to Russia found to have broken law

articles.author: Justin McCurry in Tokyo
articles.description:
Investigators probe Asahi, Kirin, Suntory and Sapporo breweries – which together control more than 90% of Japan’s beer market
Japanese authorities have raided the country’s four biggest breweries over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beer and other beverages – a practice media reports said could have forced drinkers to pay over the odds.
Officials from the Fair Trade Commission this week searched the offices of Asahi Breweries, Kirin Brewery, Suntory Beer and Sapporo Breweries – which together control more than 90% of the domestic market. The quartet are suspected of violating the anti-monopoly law.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Japan beer giants raided over suspicions they colluded to set the price of beverages

articles.author: Oliver Holmes in Bangkok and agencies
articles.description:
NGOs in Indonesian Borneo file class action lawsuit calling for government to better manage annual fires and 
The Indonesian government has been accused of “gross negligence” in a class action lawsuit over its handling of wildfires that have cloaked large parts of South-east Asia in a toxic haze, shuttered schools and caused a spike in respiratory illnesses.
The lawsuit, filed by indigenous and civil society groups in the Indonesian part of Borneo, named President Prabowo Subianto and the governor of West Kalimantan among 10 defendants. The case seeks comprehensive recovery and rehabilitation measures that would include covering the healthcare costs of residents.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Indonesia accused of ‘gross negligence’ in wildfires lawsuit as haze tests region

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
articles.description:
Pakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capital
Imran Khan’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.
The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad

articles.author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Mumbai
articles.description:
Thousands gather in Mumbai with heavy police presence as concerns mount that millions will be denied voting rights
India’s youth-led Cockroach movement kicked off more nationwide protests on Friday as thousands of people gathered in Mumbai, amid mounting concerns that millions of citizens are being unfairly stripped of their vote.
The movement, which calls itself the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) and has massive support among the country’s gen Zs, returned to the streets to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: India’s Cockroach movement launches new protests over changes to voter roll

articles.author: Megan Davies and James Michelin for MetDesk
articles.description:
Up to 300mm of rain could fall in places, while extreme downpours bring landslides and deaths in Nepal
Torrential rain and potentially damaging flooding are forecast in eastern Spain over the coming days, as cold upper air moves over the warm, humid surface air of the Mediterranean Sea, fuelling violent, slow-moving thunderstorms near Spain’s east coast. The weather pattern, known as a Dana, occurs most often in autumn.
Models show more than 100mm of rain could fall across the region on Friday, with 200-300mm possible in some areas. Cities including Valencia and Castelló de la Plana, are most at risk. Valencia has experienced several damaging floods in recent years. Catalonia has now put three towns under lockdown and Valencia has shut schools for nearly half a million children.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Eastern Spain braces for torrential rain and flooding

articles.author: Douglas Main
articles.description:
Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
A 200-year-old cottonwood tree near the US-Mexico border, known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction of Donald Trump’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it.
In late July, land defenders began a tree-sit in the ghost town of Lochiel, Arizona, taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’

articles.author: Oliver Holmes
articles.description:
US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Donald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy large quantities of Russian diesel.
The US president suggested Volodymyr Zelenskyy has not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
The tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aesthetic
Sitting behind a replica Resolute Desk, nine-year-old Sydney Wright posed for the camera like a future US president. “I love it,” she smiled. And what about the dazzling gold appliqués, gold leaf and gold trim surrounding her? “It’s cool.”
Sydney was among a steady stream of visitors on Thursday to The People’s House: A White House Experience, an interactive museum – with an orientation film narrated by The West Wing star Martin Sheen – at 1700 Pennsylvania Avenue, just 150 yards from the real thing.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DC

articles.author: Michael Sainato
articles.description:
Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote 
The president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, has easily won his re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference.
The union’s election of leadership for a four-year term began with mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election

articles.author: Chris Stein in Toledo, Ohio
articles.description:
Democrat in Congress since 1983 rebuked over ‘dangerous’ campaign ad – will it harm her chances in tight Ohio race?
Last month, Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in congressional history, released a video advertisement in which she looks directly at the camera and says exactly what she thinks about one of the most divisive issues facing Democrats today.
“Here’s the truth: I voted with Republicans to keep transgender ideology out of our schools because parents know what’s best for their kids,” Kaptur says, “and boys should not play in girls’ sports.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Marcy Kaptur: longest-serving congresswoman’s bid for another House term roiled by anti-trans ad

articles.author: Robert Tait in Washington
articles.description:
It is odd for the US defense secretary to be laying the groundwork for an event that could be organized by Tehran
Pete Hegseth’s plans to stage a public execution resemble a grotesque Iran-imitation game.
Having failed over the past seven months to defeat the Tehran regime on the battlefield, the self-styled “secretary of war” now proposes to mirror its notorious practice of enforcing the death penalty as a grand public spectacle.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: I saw Iran execute a man in public. Is this what the US wants? | Robert Tait

articles.author: Presented by Lucy Hough with Austin Sarat ; produced by Angus Neale ; senior producer Ryan Ramgobin ; executive producer Zoe Hitch
articles.description:
The execution of a former US army psychiatrist by firing squad is to be livestreamed after Pete Hegseth said it would be a public event. Nidal Hasan was sentenced to death after killing 13 people at a military base in Texas in 2009. There has been widespread condemnation of the decision, including from the UN which said it would ‘amount to torture’. Lucy Hough speaks to US academic and capital punishment specialist Austin Sarat, the author of Life After Death: Surviving Execution 
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Barbaric’ firing squad livestream ordered by Pete Hegseth - The Latest

articles.author: Judith Levine
articles.description:
Political parties vie for Jewish support based on false assumptions about a single issue: Israel
Everybody wants the Jewish vote. As if there were one. Jews are educated, generally liberal. Although they comprise only about 2% of the electorate, they vote in high numbers, overwhelmingly for Democrats. In 2024, 79% chose Kamala Harris. They are also assumed to be steadfast friends of Israel, no matter what it does. Republicans, waging a fake war on antisemitism while courting white supremacists, consider Jews increasingly up for grabs.
Nationally, Jewish Americans are concentrated in a few bright blue spots. A 2020 map from the Jewish Electorate Institute showed a third of Jews living in 20 congressional districts – out of 435 – most of them in New York, New Jersey, California and (purple) Florida. Of these, only one sent a Republican to Washington.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Stop talking about the US ‘Jewish vote’. It's not that simple | Judith Levine

articles.author: Rachel Leingang, George Chidi, David Smith, Fabiola Cineas Dani Anguianoand Ed Pilkington
articles.description:
From cost of living to the Iran war, these are the issues that matter most to US voters across the political spectrum
US voters are about to deliver their first national verdict on the second presidency of Donald Trump. On 3 November, millions of Americans will vote in midterm elections to decide control of the House of Representatives and Senate, as well as the governorships in 36 states. The results could have a huge impact on Trump’s final two years in office.
Today, the Guardian launches its 2026 midterm voter panel. Our reporters have interviewed nine voters across the country and the political spectrum about the issues that matter to them, from the cost of living, immigration and healthcare to the war in Iran and whether they trust their political leaders.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A national verdict on Trump 2.0 is coming. Nine midterm voters share where they stand

articles.author: Paul Daley
articles.description:
A proposal to livestream the killing of Nidal Hasan by firing squad opens a window ever wider to the Trump administration’s complete moral vacuity
More fool me! Here I was thinking nothing that America’s Trump administration could do or say, no matter how politically and morally bankrupt, no matter how venal or violent, was capable of shocking me any longer.
Then I woke to today’s news that one of the Trump cabinet’s bigger boofheads – the uber Christian nationalist, crusader-fantasist and “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth had announced that America would have a public firing squad execution of murderer Nidal Hasan.
Paul Daley is a Guardian Australia columnist
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Execution TV? Pete Hegseth has taken the once ‘greatest democracy’ to a horrific new low | Paul Daley

articles.author: David Smith in Washington
articles.description:
Amid a cost-of-living crisis, with US midterms a month away, the president held a ceremony to celebrate our tech overlords – again
He stands accused of being out of touch, enriching himself and his family, building a lavish White House ballroom and, with elections looming, neglecting the hardships of the voters who brought him to power.
Time for Donald Trump to show he still has the common touch? Nope.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump hosts awards party for tech billionaires, almost as if he doesn’t care about ordinary Americans

articles.author: Sam Levine in St Louis, Missouri
articles.description:
State residents express anger at Republicans who allowed chaotic voting maps saga to unfold ahead of the midterms

Sign up to The Stakes 2026: your weekly guide to the US midterms

Send us your questions on how the US economy is shaping the midterm elections

Eric Leventhal knows he’s going to vote for a Democrat in Congress when he goes to the polls in Missouri this November – the problem is he has no idea which candidate is going to be on his ballot.
In the state’s August primary, he voted for Fred Wellman, a Democrat running in the state’s second congressional district. But after a long and complicated legal battle sparked by Donald Trump’s desire to gain every advantage in the upcoming midterm contest, the districts have changed for the general election that will determine which party controls Congress. Leventhal said he lived right near the border of the first and second congressional district, so now he’s not sure which one he’s in.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Undistilled cheating’: Missouri voters furious in aftermath of Trump bid to rig electoral maps

articles.author: Nick Brown
articles.description:
A coalition of Democratic attorneys general is working to make sure voters across the spectrum have their voices heard
Elections have consequences. So do the Trump administration’s exhaustive efforts to undermine them.
Voters will be confident in their choices, but less certain whose voice will count in the face of myriad intrusions by the executive branch. A coalition of Democratic attorneys general are working to make sure voters across the political spectrum have their say.
Nick Brown is the attorney general of the state of Washington
 Continue reading...
articles.title: I’m the attorney general of Washington state. Here’s how we’re protecting the midterm elections | Nick Brown

articles.description:
Donald Trump’s latest campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, was rocked by repeated protests as the US president urged Texas voters to back the embattled Senate candidate Ken Paxton. At least half a dozen demonstrators interrupted the US president during his speech, with some led away by police. One was physically assaulted by a Trump supporter as he tried to leave the arena. The Republican campaign to maintain control of the Senate has become increasingly focused on Texas, where the Democrat James Talarico has emerged as a serious threat
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Protesters removed after disrupting Trump rally in Texas – video

articles.author: Margaret Sullivan
articles.description:
Trump seems to invent ugly new variations on his press-bashing theme almost every day
When you hate the mainstream press as much as Donald Trump does, nothing gets in the way of the punishment fantasy.
Not court rulings. Not public opinion. Not even the dreadful consequence of less media coverage.
Margaret Sullivan is a Guardian US columnist writing on media, politics and culture
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Trump’s latest attacks on the press exude desperation | Margaret Sullivan

articles.author: Hosted by Kai Wright and Carter Sherman with Charles Blow and Shrai Popat , produced by Tiara Chiaramonte , engineered by Ivan Kuraev , executive producer Rachel Humphreys
articles.description:
The biggest question in US politics may be whether Democrats can ever win in the south. In this year’s midterms, Georgia has once again emerged as a bellwether. The state has shifted from deep red to purple for the last several election cycles and remains a frontline state in the battle over voting rights. In a recent Stateside with Kai and Carter live event in collaboration with On Air Presents, hosts Kai Wright and Carter Sherman were joined by Guardian contributing writer Charles Blow and political reporter Shrai Popat for a lively conversation about everything at stake in Georgia – including why Jon Ossoff needs Keisha Lance Bottoms to win the governor’s race if he hopes to run for president in 2028, what Donald Trump might do to intervene in the election, and how any voter suppression moves could backfire in the south.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Could Trump’s plan to suppress voters backfire in the south? – Stateside with Kai and Carter

articles.author: Laure Boulinier, Sofia Couceiro and Boglarka Kosztolanyi
articles.description:
The US midterms may not be as much of a spectacle as the presidential elections, but they are just as important and can completely change not just the course of a presidential term, but federal legislation for years to come. The Guardian unpacks how these elections work, what the results mean and how they affect American life
 Continue reading...
articles.title: US midterms: what are they and why do presidents dread them? – explainer

articles.author: Matthew Taylor
articles.description:
NEU’s Daniel Kebede says earlier start times and longer summer breaks may be needed to help pupils and teachers
Schools should consider changing start and finish times, reordering holidays and moving exams from the summer months in an effort to adapt to the UK’s increasingly severe heatwaves, according to the leader of the country’s biggest education union.
Daniel Kebede, the general secretary of the National Education Union (NEU), said this summer’s repeated bouts of extreme heat had a devastating impact on teachers and pupils, as classroom temperatures topped 40C and hundreds of thousands of young people were sent home.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Retrofit schools and consider moving exams to beat extreme heat, says teaching union leader

articles.author: Aamna Mohdin Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Research challenges the notion that the growing visibility of crosses and other symbols reflects a revival of Christianity 
Christian nationalism in Britain is being driven largely by people who rarely attend church and are more concerned with defending the country’s Christian heritage, according to research.
The report, by the thinktank Theos, identified five different groups within the UK in a survey that looked at their attitudes to Christianity and Britishness.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Christian nationalism in Britain driven by people who seldom go to church, says report

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
The northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.
Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights

articles.author: Nadeem Badshah
articles.description:
Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
A man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo in Yorkshire, police have said.
Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, near Doncaster, and was set upon by the tiger.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo

articles.author: Sammy Gecsoyler
articles.description:
Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Thousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them by Israel.
The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groom appeared to be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’

articles.author: Sirin Kale
articles.description:
Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry
A paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.
In February, Vincent Chan was jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest

articles.author: Helena Horton and Michael Goodier
articles.description:
Koos Bekker’s Newt estate  encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
When South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner of Somerset to turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.
Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket of England.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’

articles.author: Chris Osuh Community affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality
They were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In the Peterloo massacre of 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.
A study by Global Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – as Robert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean

articles.author: Geneva Abdul
articles.description:
Ellie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not working
A Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote.
The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last week to treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism, and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Greens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MP

articles.author: Joanna Partridge in Cardigan
articles.description:
In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan
Worn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales.
Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales

articles.author: Dan Milmo Global technology editor
articles.description:
George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
The UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.
The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute

articles.author: Presented by Aditya Chakrabortty with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, produced by Frankie Tobi and Luke Smith; the executive producers were Maz Ebtehaj, Kirsty Major and James Tindale
articles.description:
Are we really living through ‘end times fascism’? Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor think so.
In a new series from the Guardian, the pair speak to Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty in an extended interview. From Trump 2.0 and the rise of the tech billionaire to Gaza and the climate emergency, Klein and Taylor argue we are not just lurching from crisis to crisis but are in a new and dangerous moment in history. But they haven’t given up hope of a fightback
Radical Thinking will be published every Saturday in the Politics Weekly feed
You can watch the full interview with Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor here.

 Aditya’s suggested reading:
Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor’s End Times Fascism is out now and available here. It began life as a special essay in the Guardian, which you can read here.
A different take on whether Trump 2.0 is fascist comes from the economist Branko Milanović on his brilliant Substack.
Elon Musk gives Donald Trump millions, and Trump gives Musk vast access to power. To read more, look at Quinn Slobodian and Ben Tarnoff’s Long Read for the Guardian and their recent book Muskism: a Guide for the Perplexed.
For some sensational reporting on Trump’s second term, look at Regime Change by Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan.
How did the business class learn to love Trump and embrace chaos? Paul Heideman gives a lucid analysis in his recent book Rogue Elephant.
If you want more on the new tech bros of Silicon Valley, here are four recommendations:
- In their book, Klein and Taylor regularly cite Karen Hao’s Empire of AI.
- There’s also The Nerd Reich, just out from Gil Durán.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘Gaza is a moral tear in the universe’: Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcast

articles.author: Pippa Crerar and Jessica Elgot
articles.description:
Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition
In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham.
Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: ‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget

articles.author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
articles.description:
Only ‘very small number’ of people already in Lebanon or Jordan will be referred, says organisation running scheme
The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.”
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route

articles.author: Rupert Jones
articles.description:
Competition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in years
National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.
Competition in the savings market has been growing, leading to some of the highest interest rates for years.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: UK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say experts

articles.author: Zoe Wood
articles.description:
With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry
With the Met Office warning that this year’s supersized El Niño could mean a wet and stormy winter lies ahead, it’s never been more important to maintain your home.
Payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% to £244m in 2025 amid the destruction caused by the heavy rain and strong winds that accompanied the likes of Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences

articles.author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship starts
A national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work, the government is to be told.
Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will call for a new “national pre-apprenticeship route” to offer young people further education, training and work experience.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Create new pre-apprenticeship scheme to close youth unemployment gap, says Milburn

articles.author: Rory Carroll Ireland correspondent
articles.description:
Prospect of contentious Orange Order march through Garvaghy Road in Portadown has led to a nearly two-week standoff
The Northern Ireland secretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.
Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Northern Ireland secretary Chris Bryant bans Drumcree parade

articles.author: Rowena Mason Whitehall editor
articles.description:
Tories said to be ready to fight in Clacton, with standards investigation rumoured to be nearing its end
Nigel Farage’s rivals are gearing up for a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, amid speculation that the standards inquiry into his £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.
Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight in Farage’s seat, although senior figures in the shadow cabinet are divided about whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Parties prepare for byelection in Farage seat amid speculation over £5m gift inquiry

articles.author: Presented by Peter Walker and Alexandra Topping, produced by Nada Smiljanic and Sam Gruet, music by Axel Kacoutié; the executive producer is Maz Ebtehaj
articles.description:
Zack Polanski has lost the Holborn and St Pancras byelection to Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali. Despite the Greens increasing their vote share from 2024, Polanski had the cloud of the ‘Zionism is racism’ row hanging over his head.
Now there are questions over his leadership and whether he can steer the party through the ongoing Zionism row. Will the Greens remain a fringe party?
You can watch this episode on the Politics Weekly YouTube channel here.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Did the Zionism row lose it for Zack Polanski? – podcast

articles.author: Helen Pidd, Eleanor Biggs, Laurence Topham, Ben Kape and Homa Khaleeli
articles.description:
British screenwriting royalty Russell T Davies talks to Helen Pidd about his taboo-breaking career, from rebooting Doctor Who and broadcasting explicit sex scenes in Queer as Folk to casting a trans actor in a trans role in Banana. He also reveals why he turned down James Bond, and how his views on gay representation onscreen have evolved over the years
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Russell T Davies on his groundbreaking career bringing gay joy to British TV | Today in Focus

articles.description:
Labour has seen off the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in a result that will reassure Andy Burnham and dent Zack Polanski’s position as a decisive power player on the left of British politics. In an emotional victory speech, Sagal Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, said her commitment to the constituency 'runs deep'. Polanski’s loss caps a bruising week for his party, which fell into turmoil this week after it voted to adopt a policy declaring Zionism a form of racism, raising questions about his leadership

Labour fends off Green party to win Holborn and St Pancras byelection

 Continue reading...
articles.title: 'We didn't get it over the line': Green party's Zack Polanski on byelection loss – video

articles.author: Jamie Grierson
articles.description:
Former Labour deputy leader says tech firm would work with a Reform UK government on immigration crackdowns
Tom Watson, the former Labour deputy leader who recently joined Palantir, has warned against “mob rule” when it comes to awarding public contracts.
Lord Watson, now a senior vice-president at the US tech corporation, said UK ministers could get themselves “in a lot of trouble” as he was questioned about concerns raised about the government working with his new employer.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contracts

articles.author: Dalya Alberge
articles.description:
Exclusive: Theresa Musgrove unearths newspaper archives showing one Alice Shepherd was severely punished in 1836 for similarly innocent request
Could a consumptive young woman called Alice Shepherd have been the inspiration for Oliver Twist? That is a question now being posed by a historian, who has discovered parallels between the brutality suffered by a real-life pauper incarcerated in one of Victorian London’s notorious workhouses and Charles Dickens’s fictional orphan.
In researching a new book on Dickens, Theresa Musgrove unearthed 1836 newspaper reports on Alice Shepherd, who endured starvation and solitary confinement within a workhouse in Hendon, after a magistrate ruled she was to be punished for daring to ask for permission to take a walk.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Please, sir, can I have a walk? Dickens biographer finds likely inspiration for Oliver Twist

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
It may sound odd to think Zack Polanski would be happy with second place, but after his most challenging week in politics, it could have been worse

Labour’s Abdi-Wali fends off Polanski and Greens


Parliamentary byelections can generate all sorts of emotional responses, often very strong ones. But for the main contenders in Holborn and St Pancras, the feeling this morning might be more prosaic: relief.
For Labour, Sagal Abdi-Wali’s victory with just over 45% of the total vote was widely expected, but it allows the party to credibly claim Andy Burnham as a politician able to reach people in both Reform-leaning areas such as Makerfield and in Green-friendly inner cities.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Holborn and St Pancras byelection loss will disappoint Greens – but there may also be relief

articles.author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
articles.description:
Exclusive: Badenoch’s flagship conference policy document cites £957bn estimate, twice the total in climate advisers’ data
Kemi Badenoch’s flagship party conference policy document overestimated the cost of net zero by nearly £500bn, seemingly after someone accidentally double-counted figures on a spreadsheet.
The apparent error appears in a chapter on net zero in The Right Way, a 100-page policy document produced for the Conservative conference in Birmingham. Badenoch repeatedly used the phrase in her main speech.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Tories overstate net zero cost by nearly £500bn in apparent spreadsheet error

articles.author: Denis Campbell
articles.description:
Decision by Royal College of Pharmacy to end sponsorship comes after concerns over Teva Pharmaceuticals’ ‘activities’
A second major UK health body has cut ties with an Israeli drug firm after coming under pressure from pro-Palestine campaigners.
The Royal College of Pharmacy has dropped Teva UK, the British arm of the global medicines producer Teva Pharmaceuticals, as a sponsor of and exhibitor at its annual conference next month.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Second UK health body drops Israeli drug firm after activist pressure

articles.author: Patrick Butler Social policy editor
articles.description:
Peter Fonagy lauds courage of young people and warns of consequences of rising prevalence of mental illness

Full report | NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds

Explainer | What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?

Eighteen months ago, in an off-the-cuff remark during a discussion on disability benefit cuts, Wes Streeting said mental health conditions were being “overdiagnosed”, riding headlong into another culture war.
He later apologised for the comment, but at the time it seemed the then health secretary had endorsed a populist view that ordinary stresses and disappointments had become too often medicalised, resulting in a surge of bogus clinical diagnoses and creating a “snowflake generation” of fragile, avoidant and workshy young people.
I am in awe of their courage. Young people are contending with more powerful forces than I ever faced
 Continue reading...
articles.title: No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real

articles.author: Anna Bawden Health and social affairs correspondent
articles.description:
Prof Peter Fonagy’s 607-page report is categoric that mental distress has increased substantially and ‘cannot be explained by greater awareness alone’

Full report | NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds

Analysis | No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real

The Fonagy review of NHS England’s mental health, ADHD and autism services was commissioned in 2025 by Wes Streeting, then the health secretary, in response to growing concerns that spiralling waiting lists for assessment, diagnosis and care threatened the NHS’s ability to meet the demand.
The 607-page report, published on Friday, says that without a radical overhaul, mental health and neurodiversity services will be overwhelmed. Here are some of its key findings and recommendations.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS England mental health services review: what has it found and what does it recommend?

articles.author: Denis Campbell and Anna Bawden
articles.description:
England-focused mental health review returns stark warning and calls for shift to ‘needs-led’ system

Explainer | What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?

Analysis | No ‘snowflakes’: mental health review says today’s youth have it harder and harms are real

The NHS in England is heading into a “world of system failures” as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.
The stark warning was made in a review led by Prof Peter Fonagy into the sharp rise in demand over recent decades for help with mental health and neurodevelopmental conditions.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: NHS at risk of ‘system failures’ as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds

articles.author: Esther Addley
articles.description:
Inquest hears details of how three women spent their final days but why they ended their lives may never be known
Jane Adetoro and her younger sisters, Christina and Rebecca Walters, were “the closest sisters and the best friends”, according to their family. Devoted to their father, Joseph, whom they messaged every day, the adult siblings lived quiet lives in the flat they shared in west London and would do everything together.
When they died in May this year, it was no different. Early in the morning of 13 May, the sisters’ bodies were recovered from the sea in Brighton, hours after a taxi had dropped the three women at the beachfront.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: A lake pilgrimage and a quiet car ride to the beach: last hours of sisters who took own lives in Brighton

articles.author: Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem
articles.description:
Consulate targeted in sanctions spat has unusual diplomatic status that clashes with Israel’s ambitions to fully annex the city
Israel’s attempt to close the British consulate general in Jerusalem was primarily designed to deter London from imposing sanctions on settlements in occupied Palestine. But it also served the current government’s ambitions to fully annex Jerusalem as a national capital, diplomatic and legal experts said.
The UK mission to the city has an unusual diplomatic status, which dates back to before the founding of the state of Israel, rooted in a vision of Jerusalem as a neutral enclave under international control.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: Israel’s downgrading of UK consulate aims to tighten its hold on Jerusalem

articles.author: Jillian Ambrose
articles.description:
Complaints risks putting defence ministry on collision course with Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
The Ministry of Defence has objected to at least four planned windfarms in the past year over fears the spinning blades could cause “unacceptable interference” with radars used to detect military aircraft.
MoD officials raised concerns in late June over plans for an onshore windfarm in County Durham that could result in aircraft “not being detected” within an RAF Low Flying Area, according to a letter to Britain’s planning authority.
 Continue reading...
articles.title: MoD has objected to four windfarms in past year over radar interference fears

articles.author: Michael Savage Media editor
articles.description:
Thinking Allowed, The Artificial Human and Free Thinking among other programmes hit by £500m cuts
BBC Radio 4’s consumer rights show You and Yours is to be axed after more than 50 years, becoming one of the latest victims of the corporation’s £500m cuts plan.
The programme, once described by the former Radio 4 controller Mark Damazer as “one of the most important” on the station, is one of a handful to be cut as the BBC searches for shows that can be more easily adapted as podcasts.

articles.title: BBC axes long-running Radio 4 show You and Yours in push towards podcasts

Ymarfer Byw, which was praised for its ‘musical excellence’, beat 14 other albums to the prize of £10,000
Singer-songwriter Dafydd Owain has won the 2026 Welsh music prize with his second album Ymarfer Byw.
